script.text: Eighty kilometres. That is how close Yemen's Houthis came to the port city of Aden this month, according to military sources cited by Reuters. And the same group already sits on one of the busiest shipping lanes on Earth.

If you buy anything shipped between Asia and Europe, this matters to you. Who are the Houthis? How did a movement from Yemen's northern mountains end up threatening a sea route? And how close are they now to Aden? Keep one more thing in mind: a small island in the strait that may matter more than any city.

The Houthis call themselves Ansar Allah, which means Supporters of God. The name Houthi comes from a family. The movement grew in Saada, a mountainous province in Yemen's far north, near the Saudi border. Its roots are religious. The Houthis belong to the Zaydis, a branch of Shia Islam. Zaydi imams ruled parts of Yemen for centuries, until the monarchy was overthrown in nineteen sixty-two. According to the Mapping Militants Project at Stanford, a predecessor group called Believing Youth was founded in nineteen ninety-two as a peaceful religious movement. Over the following decade, the al-Houthi family steered it toward armed struggle. The turning point came in two thousand four. Government forces killed Hussein al-Houthi, the movement's early leader. His followers took his name, and a series of wars with the government in Saada followed. Today, the Middle East Institute describes the group as a mix of religious conservatism, Yemeni nationalism and open hostility toward the United States and Israel. Iran is the key outside partner. United Nations experts have reported for years that weapons and components reach the Houthis from individuals or entities in Iran. Iran denies arming them. If you want one of these every Wednesday, subscribing is how you get it.

So how did a provincial movement take a country's capital? In September two thousand fourteen, Houthi fighters entered Sanaa and pushed out the internationally recognised government of President Abdrabbuh Mansur Hadi. They did not do it alone. Former president Ali Abdullah Saleh, once their enemy, backed them. That alliance lasted until Saleh's death in two thousand seventeen. In March two thousand fifteen, a coalition led by Saudi Arabia entered the war on the government's side. According to Reuters, the Houthis briefly got into Aden in those early months, before they were driven out. What followed was a long and devastating war. A United Nations Development Programme report projected that by the end of two thousand twenty-one, the war would have caused about three hundred seventy-seven thousand deaths, counting both fighting and indirect causes like hunger and disease. The UN has called Yemen the world's worst humanitarian crisis. The front lines froze into a rough split. The Houthis held Sanaa and much of the populated north and west. The government, backed by Saudi Arabia, held Aden and the south. For you, this was a distant war. Then the Houthis turned to the sea.

Why does a war in Yemen reach your shopping basket? Look at the map. Between Yemen and the Horn of Africa lies Bab al-Mandab, the southern gate of the Red Sea. At its narrowest it is only about twenty-six to thirty kilometres wide, depending on how it is measured. Ships heading for the Suez Canal and Europe have to pass through here. Quick question: how much oil went through this strait every day in two thousand twenty-three? Take a guess. About eight point six million barrels a day, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. In November two thousand twenty-three, after the war in Gaza began, the Houthis started attacking commercial ships. The conflict monitor ACLED counted about one hundred fifty Houthi attacks on commercial vessels in two thousand twenty-four alone. Al Jazeera reported in late two thousand twenty-five that four ships had been sunk and at least nine sailors killed. Shipping companies rerouted around the Cape of Good Hope in southern Africa, a detour of thousands of kilometres. The Energy Information Administration says oil flows through Bab al-Mandab fell to about four million barrels a day in the first eight months of two thousand twenty-four. Egypt paid too. The International Monetary Fund said the attacks cut Egypt's foreign-currency income from the Suez Canal by about six billion dollars in two thousand twenty-four. In March two thousand twenty-five, the United States launched weeks of air strikes. In May, Oman brokered a deal. The U.S. stopped bombing, and the Houthis agreed to stop attacking U.S. ships.

That could have been the end of the story. It was not. On the twenty-eighth of February two thousand twenty-six, the United States and Israel went to war with Iran. According to multiple reports, the Houthis joined in late March, firing missiles at Israel. Then they turned against a neighbour. On the twentieth of July, the Houthis announced a maritime embargo against Saudi Arabia, calling it a response to a blockade of Yemen. The timing mattered. CNBC reported that Saudi Arabia had diverted millions of barrels a day to an export terminal on its Red Sea coast. The attacks returned. The Africa Center for Strategic Studies counted twelve Houthi attacks or attempted attacks on commercial ships in the southern Red Sea since July. In August, Yemen's government said a Houthi strike on a ship in the strait killed at least six people. And then came the twist on land. In September, reports said Houthi forces took the port town of Mocha on the Red Sea coast. Time, citing sources who spoke to Reuters, reported that a day later they took Perim, the island that splits Bab al-Mandab in two. Oil prices reportedly rose above one hundred dollars a barrel. Analysts quoted by Time said that holding Mocha and Perim puts the Houthis in a stronger position to disrupt shipping, especially ships bound for Saudi Arabia.

Now the fight has moved toward Aden itself. Aden is the temporary capital of the internationally recognised government. Since early October, according to Reuters sources, the Houthis have encircled the city of Taiz, after cutting its main road south to Aden. Al Jazeera described a month-long siege that has left residents trapped. On the second of November, four military sources told Reuters that Houthi forces had advanced to within eighty kilometres of Aden. They said the Houthis had taken the whole Maqatirah district and that fighting was under way at the entrance to Tur al-Bahah, one of the main approaches to the city. Reuters could not immediately verify a Houthi video of fighters entering a nearby market. According to the same sources, that is closer than at any point since the early months of the war in two thousand fifteen. Saudi Arabia answered with air strikes on Houthi-held areas. The Houthis said those strikes killed ten people. The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted Houthi missiles and a drone aimed at southern Saudi Arabia. The government says it is pushing back. On the ninth of November, Al Jazeera reported that government forces claimed new advances, while the Houthis resumed attacks along the Saudi border. Asharq Al-Awsat reported more fighting in Al-Jawf and Marib. None of these battlefield claims can be independently checked.

So what could happen next? First, the ground war. The military sources quoted by Reuters said the advance could let the Houthis outflank government forces along the mountains that overlook Bab al-Mandab. That is where the island comes back in. Perim and the Yemeni shore opposite it frame the strait's narrow eastern channel, only about three kilometres wide. Second, the sea. The U.S. Maritime Administration says attacks on ships have become less frequent recently, but warns that the threat persists. According to the Africa Center, Saudi Arabia launched a multinational maritime security alliance in August. Insurers and shipping lines decide route by route whether the Red Sea is worth the risk. Third, the bigger war. The Houthis joined this round after the war on Iran began, so any shift between Washington and Tehran matters here too. Will Red Sea shipping be back to normal by the end of two thousand twenty-seven? Tell us in the comments: yes or no. For you, the outcome shows up in shipping times, freight costs and fuel prices, long before it shows up on a map.
Next Wednesday: how oil sanctions actually work. Price caps, shadow fleets, and who really pays when a country's oil is cut off from the market.

upload.title: Who Are the Houthis? Yemen's Rebels and the Red Sea
upload.description:
Who are Yemen's Houthis, and how did a movement from Yemen's northern mountains come to threaten one of the world's busiest shipping lanes? This explainer covers the origins of Ansar Allah in Saada, the 2014 takeover of Sanaa and the Saudi-led war, the Red Sea attacks on shipping since 2023 and their cost, the Houthis' role in the 2026 Iran war including the maritime embargo on Saudi Arabia and the reported capture of Mocha and Perim Island, and the November 2026 advance to within about 80 km of Aden reported by Reuters. Battlefield claims are attributed to their sources; unverified claims are labelled.
